• Distribute shading kits (2 Humanitarian tarpaulins, 
1 shade net, 2 bundles of rope)
• Promote double-roof systems with a 20–30 cm air 
gap, ensuring the second roof is securely anchored 
and does not overload weak shelter frames to 
prevent collapse or wind-related hazards in Gaza’s 
current context

heat

metal sections etc to support shading)
• Upgrade shelters to allow cross-ventilation by placing 
windows on opposing walls, with higher openings 
releasing rising warm air and lower openings 
admitting cooler fresh air, while aligning larger vents 
on the windward side to maximize airflow efficiency

related.title: Russia bombards Kyiv in one of war’s biggest strikes, at least 21 people killed
related.summary: The Russian Defence Ministry, in a Telegram post, said its “massive attack” using long-range, high-precision air-, land- and sea-launched weapons and drones hit military and energy facilities, as well as airports in Kyiv and other locations. Kyiv, which has stepped up strikes in recent weeks on Russia’s domestic fuel supply, said it had hit an oil refinery overnight in the Russian region of Nizhny Novgorod, where the governor reported one person killed in a strike on an industrial facility.
bullets: The Russian Defence Ministry, in a Telegram post, said its “massive attack” using long-range, high-precision air-, land- and sea-launched weapons and drones hit military and energy facilities, as well as airports in Kyiv and other locations.

We’re not even asking for more.” Russia launched 74 missiles and 496 drones overnight, the Ukrainian air force said.
The Kremlin said Russian military commanders had briefed President Vladimir Putin about the Russian attacks, adding that Moscow would continue to increase pressure on Ukraine to achieve its war aims.
Moscow said the attacks were retaliation for Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia.
related.excerpt: Russia launched hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles at Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in the early hours on Thursday, killing at least 21 people, wounding scores more and damaging around 130 buildings in one of the biggest attacks of the war. Multiple explosions shook central Kyiv and reverberated across the capital throughout the night as thousands of residents rushed to bomb shelters and underground metro stations. Huge columns of smoke filled the skyline. The attack was the deadliest in Kyiv since at least May, and the wide spread of destruction across the breadth of the capital had little precedent even in a war now in its fifth year. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who cut short his visit to Ireland and rushed home, visited a site on the city’s left bank where a nine-story residential building was half destroyed. He blamed the destruction in part on a failure of allies to deliver promised air defenses. “If our partners had delivered on their promises in a timely manner, I think we could have saved more homes and lives today,” said Zelenskiy, who looked tired and visibly frustrated. “All we ask of our partners is simply to do what we’ve agreed on. We’re not even asking for more.”

related.summary: A 61-page brief has been handed to the AFP by the Australian Centre for International Justice detailing alleged war crimes committed by an IDF battalion in Gaza across 2023 and 2024. The Australian national is named in the submission; it includes details of his service history in the IDF, his whereabouts and alleged actions during operations in 2023 and 2024, and public statements made by him during actions in Gaza.

related.title: DR Congo: Anticipatory Action and Risk Mitigation of Food Insecurity in Eastern DRC - January 2023 to May 2026
related.summary: The report covers the period from January 2023 to May 2026 and explores how humanitarian actors can move from reactive responses towards proactive risk mitigation. Nearly two-thirds of incidents (61%) involved violence against people engaged in food-related activities, including farmers working their fields, traders and marketgoers, and humanitarian workers delivering food assistance.
bullets: The report covers the period from January 2023 to May 2026 and explores how humanitarian actors can move from reactive responses towards proactive risk mitigation.

Nearly two-thirds of incidents (61%) involved violence against people engaged in food-related activities, including farmers working their fields, traders and marketgoers, and humanitarian workers delivering food assistance.

Insecurity Insight has released a new report on anticipatory action and risk mitigation for food insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, analysing how conflict-related violence continues to damage local food systems and undermine livelihoods long after individual incidents occur.
Landmines, displacement, abandoned fields and disrupted harvest cycles mean that even where incident numbers decline, food insecurity can continue to worsen months or years later.

The report argues that humanitarian responses must shift from reacting to food crises after they emerge to anticipating predictable consequences of conflict violence and acting earlier to protect livelihoods, sustain local food systems and reduce humanitarian need.

bullets: • 61% of incidents involved attacks on people carrying out food-related activities, including farmers working in agricultural fields, humanitarian workers delivering food assistance, and marketgoers.

In February 2025, for example, a farmer in Beni, North Kivu, was killed by a previously laid landmine2, illustrating the often delayed impact that one act of violence can have on livelihoods and the safety of those working within the local food system.

Similarly, the displacement of farmers from Beni in August 2025 3 will ultimately reduce agricultural production as fields were left untended and harvests were disrupted, with consequences for food production and availability.

• Local and sustainable food systems, as well as humanitarian aid, have repeatedly been subjected to a variety of conflict violence, the impacts of which compound over time and continue to undermine food security in eastern DRC today.

The cumulative pattern of incidents observed over the period highlights the sustained disruption of local food systems and livelihoods in these areas, driving increased reliance on humanitarian food-aid which is underfunded and also affected by violence and insecurity.
